title: Cyber Insurance for Small Businesses: What It Covers
description: Cyber insurance explained: incident response, downtime, data breach liability, ransomware, invoice fraud and the security conditions insurers set.
intro: If your business takes payments, stores customer data or depends on its systems, a cyber incident can mean lost income, notification costs and claims from customers. Cyber insurance pays for expert help and the financial fallout.

image.alt: Red padlock resting on a black computer keyboard

rows: Incident response, IT forensics, data restoration, business interruption, extortion (where legal).
Claims and regulatory investigations after a data breach, and media liability.
Any business that holds personal data, takes card payments or relies on IT to trade.
Insurers often ask about multi-factor authentication, backups, patching and staff training.
War and state-backed attack exclusions, social engineering sub-limits.

blocks.title: Cyber cover at a glance
covered: 24/7 incident response hotline and specialist support
Liability claims from people whose data was exposed
excluded: Failing to meet stated security conditions
Upgrading systems beyond their previous state
Losses from war or state-backed attacks, as defined

sections.html: Attackers often go after businesses with weaker defences, using phishing emails, stolen passwords and fake invoices. Even a small firm can face costs from downtime, specialist recovery work and dealing with affected customers. Cyber insurance doesn’t replace good security; it pays for help when something gets through.

• Multi-factor authentication on email and remote access.
  • Regular, tested backups kept separately from your main systems.
  • Prompt software updates and supported operating systems.
  • Staff awareness of phishing and payment-change scams.
  • Clear processes for verifying changes to supplier bank details.

In the UK, the NCSC’s Cyber Essentials scheme sets out a baseline, and some insurers recognise it. In the US, CISA publishes free guidance for small businesses. See cyber insurance basics.

Under UK GDPR and the EU GDPR, organisations must report certain personal data breaches to the regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, and tell affected people when there’s a high risk to them. US breach notification rules are set state by state. Cyber policies typically fund the legal advice and notification work.

faqs.a: Some policies cover extortion payments where legal, but many insurers and authorities discourage paying. Check the wording and the law where you operate, including sanctions rules.

faqs.q: Isn’t this covered by my business package?
faqs.a: Usually not in any meaningful way. Standard property and liability policies often exclude or barely cover cyber events.
Only if the policy includes social engineering or cyber crime cover, often with a lower sub-limit.

cardText: Incident response, downtime and liability after a cyber attack or data breach.
